u1: Let's load the box truck before noon.
u2: The small van needs to go out too.
reading_left: A extends their own original loading plan: the trailer should also be loaded before noon, like the box truck.
reading_right: A extends B's dispatch point: the trailer also needs to go out (be sent on its way), like the small van.
probe_question: What is A saying should happen to the trailer?
answer_left: It should be loaded before noon.
answer_right: It also needs to be dispatched.
notes: Stripping fragment 'And the trailer' takes its predicate from the nearest clause under right bracketing ('needs to go out'), echoing B; left bracketing reaches back to u1's 'load ... before noon'. Recency and the additive 'too/and' parallelism favor right; explicit mention of the noon deadline in u3 would force left.
response_left: The trailer should also be loaded before noon, like the box truck.
response_right: The trailer also needs to go out, like the small van.

u1: I've stopped taking the elevator at work.
reading_left: A specifies when they stopped taking the elevator: they have avoided it since Tuesday.
reading_right: A dates the change B implied: the stairs have been the quicker option since Tuesday (e.g. the elevator slowed or broke down then).
answer_right: The stairs became the quicker route.
notes: The adjunct fragment 'Since Tuesday' most naturally fills the temporal slot of A's own prior clause (stopped taking the elevator). The right reading requires accommodating an event that made the stairs quicker; a follow-up like 'it broke on Tuesday' would push right.
response_left: A stopped taking the elevator on Tuesday.
response_right: The stairs became the quicker option on Tuesday.

u1: Has the invoice gone out yet?
reading_left: A draws the conclusion that answers their own question: the invoice has not been sent, so the answer is no.
reading_right: A completes B's status report into a fuller description: the invoice is drafted and saved but not sent.
probe_question: In the last turn, is A answering the original question or finishing B's description?
answer_left: Answering the original question: no, it has not gone out.
answer_right: Finishing B's description of the invoice's state.
notes: Elliptical 'But not sent' has the same propositional content under both bracketings but a different discourse function: under left it closes A's question with an inferred answer; under right it is a cooperative completion of B's clause. Intonation (falling vs. listing) would disambiguate in speech.
response_left: Answering the original question: no, it hasn't gone out.
response_right: Finishing B's description of the invoice's status.

u1: Does your knee hurt when you climb stairs?
u2: It mostly bothers me in the morning.
reading_left: The doctor opens a new line of questioning, asking about a different trigger: whether the knee hurts after exercise.
reading_right: The doctor checks the pattern the patient just stated: confirming that the pain is limited to mornings and does not occur after exercise.
probe_question: Is the doctor's last turn introducing a new scenario or confirming the patient's stated pattern?
answer_left: Introducing a new scenario (pain after exercise).
notes: Sluice-like 'Not after exercise?' under right bracketing is a confirmation check of the patient's 'mostly in the morning'; under left it is a fresh diagnostic question expanding beyond the stated pattern. Fictional low-stakes check-up context; a preceding 'And' ('And not after exercise?') would favor the confirmation reading.
response_left: Confirming the patient's stated pattern: morning pain, not after exercise.
response_right: Introducing a new scenario: asking whether exercise also triggers pain.

u1: Priya volunteered to present the product demo.
u2: Marcus already volunteered for the workshop.
reading_left: Lena, like Priya, volunteered to present the product demo.
reading_right: Lena, like Marcus, volunteered for the workshop.
notes: Classic VP-ellipsis ambiguity: 'did' can take 'volunteered to present the product demo' (u1) or 'volunteered for the workshop' (u2) as antecedent. Recency favors the workshop, discourse parallelism (volunteering announcements) keeps the demo live; a cooperative listener has no decisive cue.
response_left: Lena volunteered to present the product demo, like Priya.
response_right: Lena volunteered for the workshop, like Marcus.

u1: You usually pick up Emma from practice on Thursdays.
u2: I have a dentist appointment this Thursday.
reading_left: Dad also usually picks up Emma on Thursdays, so he can cover this week — A is offering a solution.
reading_right: Dad also has a dentist appointment this Thursday, so he is unavailable too — A is adding another problem.
probe_question: Is Dad available to pick up Emma this Thursday?
answer_left: Yes, he does the Thursday pickup too.
answer_right: No, he has a dentist appointment too.
notes: 'Does too' is VP ellipsis with two candidate antecedents: 'picks up Emma on Thursdays' (u1) and 'has a dentist appointment this Thursday' (u2). Recency and the shared 'this Thursday' frame strongly favor right; left requires treating u2 as a parenthetical obstacle and resuming the pickup topic.
response_left: Yes — Dad also usually picks up Emma on Thursdays.
response_right: No — Dad also has a dentist appointment this Thursday.

u1: I booked the back room for the party.
u2: The main hall fits more people.
reading_left: A adds a detail about their booking: the back room was booked for eighty people.
reading_right: A counters B's objection: we only need space for eighty, so the main hall's extra capacity does not matter.
probe_question: What is A doing in the last turn?
answer_left: Specifying the size of the back-room booking.
answer_right: Arguing the back room is big enough.
notes: Fragment 'For eighty, though' — the concessive 'though' under right bracketing marks contrast with B's 'fits more people' (capacity is beside the point). Under left it merely elaborates the booking fact, and 'though' has nothing to contrast with, which is why right is the cooperative reading.
response_left: Defending the booking: the back room suffices for eighty guests.
response_right: Conceding B's point: the main hall is needed for eighty.

u1: Should we take the morning train to Glasgow?
reading_left: A sticks to the original plan: the morning train works for them, despite the price difference.
reading_right: A accepts B's suggestion: taking the cheaper evening train works for them.
probe_question: Which train does A agree to take?
notes: The elided subject of 'Works for me' is recovered as 'the morning train' under left (u3 responds to the whole exchange by reaffirming u1's proposal) or 'the evening one' under right (u3 closes the proposal-acceptance pair with u2). Acceptance of the immediately preceding suggestion is the default; left needs contrastive stress ('The MORNING one works for me').
response_left: The morning train, accepting the original proposal.
response_right: The evening train, accepting B's cheaper suggestion.

u1: Marketing gets the corner office this quarter.

notes: Bare fragment 'And finance' can be a subject remnant for either 'gets the corner office this quarter' (u1) or 'asked for it first' (u2). Both are coherent workplace moves (expanding an allocation vs. piling on a grievance); only world knowledge about how many offices exist would push a listener one way.
response_left: Finance also gets the corner office this quarter.
response_right: Finance also asked for the corner office first.

u1: A package arrived for you this morning.
reading_left: A specifies where the package came from: it was sent from Lisbon.
reading_right: A restricts B's claim: B wasn't expecting anything from Lisbon (though B may have been expecting packages from elsewhere).
probe_question: Was B expecting a package from anywhere at all?
answer_left: No, B expected nothing; the package simply came from Lisbon.
answer_right: Possibly yes — just not from Lisbon.
notes: PP fragment 'From Lisbon' under left modifies 'package arrived' (origin of the delivery). Under right it attaches inside B's negative clause, scoping the expectation: 'wasn't expecting anything from Lisbon' implicates expectations of other origins. The left attachment is the default modification of the most salient object; right needs a contrastive context (e.g. B is a collector awaiting several parcels).
response_left: No — B expected nothing at all; it merely came from Lisbon.
response_right: Yes — B expected nothing from Lisbon, but possibly from elsewhere.
